rationale: A limit is defined as a limit *of a function*; the function concept is presupposed.
The derivative is defined as the limit of a difference quotient.
The Riemann integral is defined as the limit of Riemann sums.
An antiderivative is, by definition, a function whose derivative equals the given function.
FTC states the equivalence between antiderivatives and definite integrals; antiderivatives are presupposed.
FTC relates the definite integral to antidifferentiation; the integral concept is presupposed.
A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative taken while holding other variables constant; the ordinary derivative is presupposed.
An ODE is an equation relating a function to its derivatives; without the derivative concept the equation has no content.
The dot product is a binary operation on vectors; vectors are presupposed.
The cross product is a binary operation on vectors in three dimensions; vectors are presupposed.
Velocity is defined as a rate of change with respect to time; time is presupposed.
Velocity is the time derivative of position; position is presupposed.
Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity; velocity is presupposed.
In continuous mechanics, velocity is defined as dx/dt — the derivative of position with respect to time. The derivative concept is required to even state what velocity means.
Acceleration is dv/dt, the derivative of velocity with respect to time.
Velocity is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction); the vector concept is required to distinguish it from speed.
Acceleration is a vector quantity.
Force is a vector quantity; Newtonian mechanics treats forces as vectors that add componentwise.
Work is defined as the line integral of force over displacement; the integral concept is required.
Newton's second law in its dynamical form F = m·d²x/dt² is a second-order ODE; the ODE concept is required to state and solve it.
Torque is defined as τ = r × F, the cross product of position and force.
Newton's second law relates net force to mass times acceleration; mass is one of its terms.
Newton's second law expresses force in terms of mass and acceleration; force is the equation's subject.
Newton's second law relates net force to mass times acceleration; acceleration is one of its terms.
Work is defined as the action of a force over a displacement; the force concept is required.
Kinetic energy is defined via the work-energy theorem (work done equals change in kinetic energy); rigorously defining KE goes through work.
The conservation principle exchanges kinetic for other energy forms; KE is one of the terms it conserves.
The conservation principle exchanges potential for other energy forms; PE is one of the terms it conserves.
Momentum is defined as mass times velocity; mass is one of its terms.
Momentum is defined as mass times velocity; velocity is one of its terms.
The conservation principle conserves momentum specifically; the momentum concept is presupposed.
Torque is the rotational analogue of force, defined as r × F; the force concept is required.
Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass, computed from a mass distribution.
Angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity; moment of inertia is one of its terms.
Angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity; angular velocity is one of its terms.
The gravitational force law has the masses of the two bodies as its principal terms.
The law specifies a force; the force concept is presupposed.
Friction is a kind of contact force.
A normal force is a kind of contact force.
Kinetic energy is a kind of energy.
Potential energy is a kind of energy.
Trigonometric functions are mathematical functions.
